dedupe_keys.name: proposed natural gas pipelines and environmental justice in the united states penn state

description: This study by Julia Strube, Brian Thiede and co-authors at the Pennsylvania State University, published in the Journal of Rural Studies in 2021, asks whether proposed natural gas transmission pipelines in the United States are routed through census tracts with more minority, low-income or rural residents. It combines the 2015 five-year American Community Survey with pipeline route data compiled by the FracTracker Alliance for pipelines permitted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) whose planned routes were published, and fits binary logistic regressions at tract level. The results give only limited and sometimes contradictory support to environmental justice expectations: a higher share of highly educated residents lowers the likelihood of a proposal, but so does a higher poverty rate, and only the shares of Black and Asian residents are significantly (negatively) associated. Coverage: the contiguous US tracts crossed by the proposed routes studied. Format and access: the article's full text on PubMed Central. Licence and cost: publisher copyright, free to read in PMC. Caveats: the authors note that routes of built pipelines are confidential in the US, so the study covers proposals only. It shows how hazard exposure and equity can be built into pipeline siting and resilience planning. It relates to the National Pipeline Mapping System and the CDC Social Vulnerability Index in the catalogue.
